tagline: Two hills, one century: Tel Aviv's leafy hilltop neighbour
lines: Givatayim means 'two hills' in Hebrew: Borochov Hill and Kozlovsky Hill.
The town has since grown to cover four hills, adding Rambam and the Railway Workers' hill.
Kozlovsky Hill rises about 85 m, one of the highest points in the whole Gush Dan area.
It all began on 2 April 1922, when 22 pioneers laid the first stone of Borochov.
Borochov is called the country's first workers' neighbourhood.
Its co-op grocery, the 'Tzarchania', later grew into the Blue Square supermarket chain.
Israel's first public swimming pool opened on Rambam Hill in 1945.
Kozlovsky Hill has hosted Israel's largest public observatory since 1968.
In December 1917, Ottoman and ANZAC troops fought a battle on Kozlovsky Hill.
Chalcolithic burial ossuaries were dug up on Kozlovsky Hill in 1958.
Neighbourhoods merged into a council in 1942; Givatayim became a city in December 1959.
About 58,000 people live on just over 3 square km: one of Israel's densest cities.
Katznelson Street has turned into a buzzing strip of cafes and wine bars.
The Shalom Lookout on Kozlovsky Hill is a favourite spot for views over Tel Aviv.
known_for: Its hills, especially Kozlovsky Hill and the Shalom Lookout
The Givatayim Observatory, Israel's largest public observatory
Borochov, the country's first workers' neighbourhood
Katznelson Street's bar and cafe scene
Givatayim Mall (2005) and the 35-dunam Givatayim Park (2008)
Givatayim Theatre and the Thelma Yellin arts school
history: 1917: Ottoman and ANZAC forces clash on Kozlovsky Hill
1922: Borochov, the first workers' neighbourhood, is founded on 2 April
1925: Shenkin neighbourhood founded, mostly craftsmen and small traders
1931: Railway Workers' neighbourhood built with Bank Hapoalim's help
1933-1936: Rambam, Kozlovsky, Kiryat Yosef and Arlozorov neighbourhoods follow
1942: the neighbourhoods are joined under one local council
1959: Givatayim is declared a city on 10 December
1968: the observatory opens on Kozlovsky Hill
2005: Givatayim Mall opens; Givatayim Park follows in 2008

neighbourhoods.name: Borochov
neighbourhoods.mood: The 1922 birthplace: socialist pioneers, the first co-op shop, the central library

neighbourhoods.name: Shenkin
neighbourhoods.mood: Founded by craftsmen and small traders; its street now hosts wine bars and delis

neighbourhoods.name: Rambam (Givat Rambam)
neighbourhoods.mood: Hill with the old water tower, the first public pool and the Givatayim Theatre

neighbourhoods.name: Kozlovsky Hill
neighbourhoods.mood: Hilltop with a reservoir, the observatory, a garden and the Shalom Lookout

neighbourhoods.name: Kiryat Yosef
neighbourhoods.mood: Quiet streets around the Tikva Garden and the town's memorial to fallen soldiers

neighbourhoods.name: Arlozorov
neighbourhoods.mood: 1936 neighbourhood slowed for years by land never split into private plots

neighbourhoods.name: Railway Workers (Poalei HaRakevet)
neighbourhoods.mood: A 1931 housing experiment for workers without means

neighbourhoods.name: Teachers' Housing (Shikun HaMorim)
neighbourhoods.mood: Two-storey houses with outdoor stairs around a big shared garden

streets.HaShalom: Derech HaShalom, 'Peace Road': the city's entrance and a main way into Tel Aviv
streets.Ben Gurion: Named for David Ben-Gurion, Israel's first prime minister
streets.Yitzhak Rabin: Named for the PM murdered in 1995; a pedestrian suspension bridge crosses it
streets.Moshe Dayan: Tel Aviv road for the general; once 'Victory Road', it runs on as Aliyat HaNoar
streets.Katznelson: For Labour Zionist leader Berl Katznelson; the main street and nightlife spine
streets.Aluf Sadeh: For Gen. Yitzhak Sadeh, Palmach founder; a busy 2.6 km road on the Ramat Gan side
streets.Arlosoroff: For Haim Arlosoroff, Zionist leader shot on a Tel Aviv beach in 1933
streets.Zeev Jabotinsky: For Revisionist Zionist leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky; No. 48 is a historic building
streets.Menachem Begin: Tel Aviv road named for PM Begin in 2001 (was Petah Tikva Road); past Azrieli
streets.Uziel: For Rabbi Ben-Zion Uziel, first Sephardi chief rabbi of the State of Israel
streets.HaTayasim: 'The Pilots': beside Ramat HaTayasim, honouring 3 airmen killed defending Tel Aviv
streets.Aliyat HaNoar: For Youth Aliyah, which saved Jewish children from the Nazis; on the Tel Aviv border
streets.Weizmann: For Chaim Weizmann, Israel's first president; post office and bars near Katznelson
streets.Yigal Alon: Tel Aviv street for the Palmach commander and minister; office towers line it
streets.Arvey Nahal: 'Willows of the Brook': edges Nahalat Yitzhak beside the Givatayim line

food: Sabich (pita with fried aubergine and egg) from Oved's famous stand
Wine bars and cocktail bars along Katznelson Street
Falafel at the busy Katznelson and Weizmann corner
Deli by day, wine bar by night on Shenkin Street
Cafes and chain coffee spots around the town centre
rhythm: Traffic piles up on the big entry roads like Aluf Sadeh and HaShalom, which carry commuters into Tel Aviv. By night Katznelson Street fills with young locals and visitors at its bars, and street parking gets tight. As across Israel, shops and traffic thin out from Friday afternoon until Saturday evening.
